blocks.text: Dates are deceptively one of the trickiest data types to clean correctly. The same calendar date can be written dozens of visually different but valid ways, and getting the parsing wrong silently corrupts every value rather than raising an error.

items: Multiple formats mixed in the same column: "2023-01-15", "01/15/2023", and "Jan 15, 2023" all appearing together.
The US versus rest of world day and month ambiguity: "03/04/2023" means March 4th in the US convention but April 3rd almost everywhere else.
Dates stored as plain strings/text instead of an actual datetime type.
Timezone information missing or inconsistent, some timestamps naive and others timezone aware in the same column.

code.content:
pd.to_datetime(df['date'], format='%Y-%m-%d')     # explicit format, fast and safe
pd.to_datetime(df['date'], dayfirst=True)            # resolve US vs international ambiguity
pd.to_datetime(df['date'], errors='coerce')          # unparseable values become NaT, not a crash

blocks.text: The format parameter tells pandas the exact expected format rather than guessing, which is both faster and safer. The dayfirst parameter helps resolve the US versus international ambiguity when the format is not fully explicit. errors='coerce' turns unparseable dates into NaT, pandas' null value for datetimes, rather than crashing the whole operation.

A "signup_date" column contains three different format styles in the same column. Naively assuming one single format silently fails or produces wrong results for the other rows, while pandas' format="mixed" option, built for exactly this situation, correctly parses all three.

code.content:
dates = pd.Series(['2023-01-15', '01/20/2023', 'Feb 3, 2023'])
parsed = pd.to_datetime(dates, format='mixed', dayfirst=False)
print(parsed)
# 0   2023-01-15
# 1   2023-01-20
# 2   2023-02-03

df['ts'] = df['ts'].dt.tz_localize('UTC')            # attach a timezone to naive timestamps
df['ts_local'] = df['ts'].dt.tz_convert('US/Eastern') # convert an already aware timestamp

blocks.title: Why comparisons can fail
blocks.content: Comparing a naive and a timezone aware timestamp directly raises an error in pandas. This is a deliberate safety feature, not a bug, comparing them without accounting for timezone would silently give a wrong answer.

blocks.text: 5. Extracting Features From a Clean Column
Once a column is properly parsed as a real datetime, the .dt accessor unlocks useful components directly.

code.content:
df['year'] = df['signup_date'].dt.year
df['month'] = df['signup_date'].dt.month
df['weekday'] = df['signup_date'].dt.dayofweek
df['hour'] = df['signup_date'].dt.hour

blocks.text: This is a forward pointer to feature engineering, covered more deeply in the Machine Learning Fundamentals course.

A useful sanity check flags dates that are logically impossible: birth dates in the future, or timestamps before a system's known launch date, are almost always data entry errors, similar in spirit to the invalid values topic but specific to date logic.

items: Trusting automatic guessing on a large ambiguous dataset without spot checking the results, a single wrongly guessed row can silently corrupt an entire downstream calculation.
Mixing naive and timezone aware timestamps in the same column without normalizing first, which causes silent incorrect comparisons or explicit errors depending on the operation.
Convert every date column to a real datetime type, never leave it as text.
Use an explicit format or format="mixed" rather than blind automatic guessing on ambiguous data.
Resolve day first versus month first ambiguity explicitly.
Normalize timezone handling before comparing timestamps.
Validate that parsed dates fall within a plausible range.
